title: Later Alligator: Sweet Geraldine and character-specific reactions

people.name: Lindsay Small-Butera
people.role: Director; writing, concepting, storyboarding, animation and design (self-described in interview)

people.name: Alex Small-Butera
people.role: Keyframer; animation and design (described by Lindsay in joint interview)

summary: Large directional eyes and a small curved mouth make a boastful dialogue pose legible without a large facial rig.

observations.text: In the inspected Sweet Geraldine frame, huge eyes look upward while the small mouth curves up toward the snout. A fang and tilted face add personality; the pose reads alongside her boast about being a claw-machine mastermind.
Lindsay says the reaction sets were decided case by case around each alligator's conversation nodes, with shared categories including wins, losses, happy, sad, disappointed and angry.
The duo describe getting the feeling of the gesture down rapidly and refining it in later passes. Alex describes exporting labeled PNG sequences from Harmony for assembly in Unity.

mistIdeas: Our inference: give MIST distinct confident, sheepish and uncertain resting mouth shapes before adding movement. The eyes should establish attention, with the mouth providing attitude.
Our inference: author reactions to concrete events such as recognition, misunderstanding and successful completion. Reuse broad emotion categories but choose a different held pose for each event.

title: Smile For Me: Putunia and Jerafina response comparisons

people.name: Yugo Limbo
people.role: Co-creator (official press credits); animator, game developer and comic artist (official studio biography)

people.name: Day Lane
people.role: Co-creator (official press credits); producer, programmer and gameplay designer (official studio biography)

summary: Official side-by-side nod/shake GIFs connect expression references directly to a player's conversational response.

observations.text: The sampled Putunia frame pairs a small, clenched-looking mouth and intense narrow eyes with a raised boxing glove and question marks. The body and face both support the confrontational line.
The sampled Jerafina frame uses a tilted face, conspicuous lips, a relaxed seated pose and crossed legs for a very different conversational attitude from Putunia.

The official page supplies comparison GIFs named for nod/shake responses. The press history attributes the nod-and-shake controls to Day and the collage-art and live-action puppetry direction to Yugo.

mistIdeas: Our inference: design separate acknowledging and declining responses. A nod should settle into attentive eyes, while a decline could use a small sideways gaze and a restrained mouth instead of a universal happy bounce.
Our inference: retain a little character attitude during interaction. The same input can have more personality than a generic checkmark.

title: Great God Grove: contrasting god faces

people.name: Yugo Limbo
people.role: Developer (with Day Lane); animator in official studio biography

summary: A supplied god-dialogue GIF juxtaposes very different face designs while keeping the speaking face large and readable.

observations.text: One sampled frame pairs a long green face with closed angled eyelids on the left and a round orange face with star-shaped eyes and a small pinched mouth on the right. The compact mouth marks contrast with very different eye silhouettes.
The official press kit specifically credits Jack Cornish for 3d animations; it credits Day Lane and Yugo Limbo as developers.

mistIdeas: Our inference: test emotional eye silhouettes independently from mouth size. Small closed or pinched mouths can carry a feeling when the lids or pupils already establish it.
Our inference: include at least one inward-looking pose with closed angled lids. Keep it visually different from an ordinary blink.

title: Thank Goodness You're Here!: Pip Williamson's hybrid character workflow

people.name: Pip Williamson
people.role: Animation team lead; character, interactive and stylised animation

summary: A named animation lead explains how to preserve drawn poses when implementing character animation in an engine.

observations.text: Pip says the team began with free-drawn roughs, then used a hybrid workflow combining in-engine animation and replacement sprites where position, rotation and scale were insufficient.
Her portfolio says this retained snappy movements from the frame-by-frame roughs, and identifies her work animating over 200 game elements and leading the animation team.

mistIdeas: Our inference: sketch MIST's extreme mouth and eyelid poses first, then decide which transitions need replacement drawings. Do not force every expression through interpolation of one neutral shape.
Our inference: compare rough expression changes against the final engine playback so implementation convenience does not erase the pose contrast.
